results.name: uniform_digit_set_same_parity_yes
results.description: In sets of >=2 examples that all share one final digit, yes rate for targets of the same parity but a different final digit (not examples); t_observed below null_mean means people apply the shared-final-digit rule more sharply than the model's partial parity credit (model over-produces yes for parity-only matches).
results.code:
# name: uniform_digit_set_same_parity_yes
# description: In sets of >=2 examples that all share one final digit, yes rate for targets of the same parity but a different final digit (not examples); t_observed below null_mean means people apply the shared-final-digit rule more sharply than the model's partial parity credit (model over-produces yes for parity-only matches).
def test_statistic(df):
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    sel = np.zeros(len(t), bool)
    for s in np.unique(sets):
        xs = np.array([int(v) for v in s.split(",")])
        if len(xs) < 2 or len(np.unique(xs % 10)) != 1:
            continue
        m = sets == s
        tt = t[m]
        d0 = xs[0] % 10
        sel[m] = ((tt % 2) == (d0 % 2)) & ((tt % 10) != d0)
    if sel.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].astype(float).values[sel].mean())

results.name: trial_index_yes_slope
results.description: OLS slope of rating on trial_index, in change of yes-probability per 100 trials; t_observed above null_mean (~0) means people drift toward saying yes more over the session, which the stationary model cannot produce (below = drift toward no).

results.name: set_yes_rate_dispersion
results.description: SD across number_sets of the set-level yes rate (targets that are not examples); t_observed above null_mean means people's overall generalization breadth differs more between sets (some sets almost all-no, others almost all-yes) than the model's features produce.
results.code:
# name: set_yes_rate_dispersion
# description: SD across number_sets of the set-level yes rate (targets that are not examples); t_observed above null_mean means people's overall generalization breadth differs more between sets (some sets almost all-no, others almost all-yes) than the model's features produce.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    padded = "," + sets.str.replace(" ", "") + ","
    in_set = np.array([p.find("," + str(v) + ",") >= 0 for p, v in zip(padded.values, t.values)])
    d = df.loc[~in_set]
    rates = d.groupby("number_set")["rating"].mean()
    if len(rates) < 2:
        return 0.0
    return float(rates.std())

results.name: last_vs_first_example_digit_match_gap
results.description: In multi-example sets, among non-example targets sharing a final digit with exactly one example, yes rate when that example was shown last minus when it was shown first; t_observed different from null_mean (~0) means presentation order matters (above = recency, below = primacy), which the order-free model cannot produce.
results.code:
# name: last_vs_first_example_digit_match_gap
# description: In multi-example sets, among non-example targets sharing a final digit with exactly one example, yes rate when that example was shown last minus when it was shown first; t_observed different from null_mean (~0) means presentation order matters (above = recency, below = primacy), which the order-free model cannot produce.
def test_statistic(df):
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    pos = np.full(len(t), -1)
    for s in np.unique(sets):
        xs = np.array([int(v) for v in s.split(",")])
        if len(xs) < 2:
            continue
        m = sets == s
        tt = t[m]
        match = (tt[:, None] % 10) == (xs[None, :] % 10)
        isex = (tt[:, None] == xs[None, :]).any(1)
        one = (match.sum(1) == 1) & ~isex
        idx = match.argmax(1)
        p = np.where(one, np.where(idx == len(xs) - 1, 1, np.where(idx == 0, 0, -1)), -1)
        pos[m] = p
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    last = pos == 1
    first = pos == 0
    if last.sum() == 0 or first.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[last].mean() - r[first].mean())

results.name: wide_band_unmatched_in_band_yes
results.description: In sets whose examples span >=5 decades, yes rate for in-band non-example targets sharing no final digit and not a common-factor multiple; t_observed below null_mean means the model over-extends full leading-digit familiarity across wide bands (people do not treat a wide empty band as familiar), above means it under-produces it.
results.code:
# name: wide_band_unmatched_in_band_yes
# description: In sets whose examples span >=5 decades, yes rate for in-band non-example targets sharing no final digit and not a common-factor multiple; t_observed below null_mean means the model over-extends full leading-digit familiarity across wide bands (people do not treat a wide empty band as familiar), above means it under-produces it.
def test_statistic(df):
    from functools import reduce
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    sel = np.zeros(len(t), bool)
    for s in np.unique(sets):
        xs = np.array([int(v) for v in s.split(",")])
        lo, hi = (xs // 10).min(), (xs // 10).max()
        if hi - lo < 5:
            continue
        g = reduce(math.gcd, [int(v) for v in xs])
        m = sets == s
        tt = t[m]
        dig = ((tt[:, None] % 10) == (xs[None, :] % 10)).any(1)
        isex = (tt[:, None] == xs[None, :]).any(1)
        cf = (g >= 3) & (tt % max(g, 1) == 0)
        inb = (tt // 10 >= lo) & (tt // 10 <= hi)
        sel[m] = inb & ~dig & ~isex & ~cf
    if sel.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].astype(float).values[sel].mean())

results.name: single_example_adjacent_decade_unmatched_yes
results.description: In single-example sets, yes rate for targets one decade away from the example that share neither its final digit nor its parity; t_observed above null_mean means the model under-produces generalization from one example to nearby numbers of opposite parity (a broad-magnitude hypothesis), below means it over-produces it.
results.code:
# name: single_example_adjacent_decade_unmatched_yes
# description: In single-example sets, yes rate for targets one decade away from the example that share neither its final digit nor its parity; t_observed above null_mean means the model under-produces generalization from one example to nearby numbers of opposite parity (a broad-magnitude hypothesis), below means it over-produces it.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~sets.str.contains(",").values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    x = pd.to_numeric(sets.where(single, "0"), errors="coerce").fillna(0).astype(int).values
    sel = single & (np.abs(t // 10 - x // 10) == 1) & ((t % 2) != (x % 2))
    if sel.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].astype(float).values[sel].mean())

results.name: in_band_proximity_gap
results.description: Among in-band targets sharing no final digit with any example (not examples), yes rate for targets within 4 of some example minus targets >=10 from every example; t_observed above null_mean means the model under-produces fine-grained numeric-proximity generalization, below means people favour in-band targets far from the examples more than the model (it gives all in-band targets the same magnitude boost).
results.code:
# name: in_band_proximity_gap
# description: Among in-band targets sharing no final digit with any example (not examples), yes rate for targets within 4 of some example minus targets >=10 from every example; t_observed above null_mean means the model under-produces fine-grained numeric-proximity generalization, below means people favour in-band targets far from the examples more than the model (it gives all in-band targets the same magnitude boost).
def test_statistic(df):
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    uniq = df["number_set"].astype(str).unique()
    info = {}
    for s in uniq:
        xs = np.array([int(v) for v in s.split(",")])
        info[s] = xs
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    mind = np.empty(len(t)); dig = np.zeros(len(t), bool); inband = np.zeros(len(t), bool)
    for s in uniq:
        m = sets == s
        xs = info[s]
        tt = t[m]
        diff = np.abs(tt[:, None] - xs[None, :])
        mind[m] = diff.min(1)
        dig[m] = ((tt[:, None] % 10) == (xs[None, :] % 10)).any(1)
        lo, hi = (xs // 10).min(), (xs // 10).max()
        inband[m] = (tt // 10 >= lo) & (tt // 10 <= hi)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    base = inband & ~dig & (mind > 0)
    near = base & (mind <= 4)
    far = base & (mind >= 10)
    if near.sum() == 0 or far.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near].mean() - r[far].mean())

results.name: factor_rule_gap_outside_band
results.description: In sets with common factor >=3, among non-example targets outside the decade band sharing no final digit with any example, yes rate for multiples of the common factor minus non-multiples; t_observed above null_mean means people apply the factor rule regardless of magnitude more strongly than the model's additive logit boost allows (below = weaker).
results.code:
# name: factor_rule_gap_outside_band
# description: In sets with common factor >=3, among non-example targets outside the decade band sharing no final digit with any example, yes rate for multiples of the common factor minus non-multiples; t_observed above null_mean means people apply the factor rule regardless of magnitude more strongly than the model's additive logit boost allows (below = weaker).
def test_statistic(df):
    from functools import reduce
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    grp = np.full(len(t), -1)
    for s in np.unique(sets):
        xs = np.array([int(v) for v in s.split(",")])
        g = reduce(math.gcd, [int(v) for v in xs])
        if g < 3:
            continue
        lo, hi = (xs // 10).min(), (xs // 10).max()
        m = sets == s
        tt = t[m]
        dig = ((tt[:, None] % 10) == (xs[None, :] % 10)).any(1)
        outb = (tt // 10 < lo) | (tt // 10 > hi)
        ok = outb & ~dig
        grp[m] = np.where(ok, (tt % g == 0).astype(int), -1)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    a = grp == 1
    b = grp == 0
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
